flags.concern: A pool of 20 per process may be more connections than the database allows.
Eight workers could overload the CPU on the current instance size.
pool_pre_ping adds a round trip to every checkout.

findings.title: Larger pools do not add request concurrency
findings.explanation: A synchronous worker handles one request at a time and this code uses one connection per request. It can reuse one connection, so raising each pool to 20 plus 20 overflow does not increase request concurrency. The 8 x 40 = 320 figure is a configured upper bound, not actual demand. Measure active connections and query time before treating the pool limit as the bottleneck.

findings.title: Pool wait is not a query timeout
findings.explanation: pool_timeout limits waiting for a pool checkout. It does not limit query execution or waiting for a free Gunicorn worker. With one returned checkout per synchronous worker, normal requests do not fill this pool. Raising the timeout therefore does not address the stated slowdown. If pool waiting is later demonstrated, align it with request and worker deadlines instead of assuming a longer wait fixes it.

findings.title: More workers need workload evidence
findings.explanation: Changing four synchronous workers to eight permits up to eight concurrent request checkouts under the stated model, not 320. More query concurrency can increase database load, but an outage is not established by these settings. Measure throughput, query latency, CPU, and other clients before choosing this worker count.
